messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele was a 31-year-old professor, married, who came to treatment months after a life-threatening car crash that she still could not tell in a straight line. She remembered driving home after teaching, the late light flashing across the windshield, and then one piercing instant of absolute clarity: another car suddenly crossing into her lane. After that, her recollection broke apart. There was the violent image of metal folding and glass bursting inward, then nothing she could place, then a sharp fragment of her own hands gripping the wheel, then blankness again. When people asked what happened, including her husband and later colleagues who knew she had been injured, she would begin, get stuck, lose the thread, and stop. Some moments felt burned into her mind with unbearable vividness, while whole stretches were missing, and the disconnected quality of the memory left her feeling as if the worst thing that had happened to her existed in pieces she could neither assemble nor trust.

That broken quality of remembering had started to shape what she believed about herself and her life. Because she could not hold the event together in a coherent account, Mele had come to feel that something essential in her had been damaged. Once she had concluded that her life no longer made sense and that she no longer really belonged in it, ordinary cues began to snag on that belief and turn into reminders: traffic updates on the radio before class, a colleague mentioning a commute, even the faculty parking lot at dusk could suddenly feel charged with the crash. She used to think of herself as engaged, intellectually alive, and at home in the world of her department, her marriage, and her friendships. Now she described herself as always miserable. She felt estranged even in familiar places, as though she no longer belonged anywhere, not fully with her students, not fully with her husband, not even fully inside her own life. The blank spaces in memory made the whole experience feel senseless to her, and from there it was a short step to the conviction that nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore.

Those beliefs fed directly into the way she lived in a state of danger. Because she no longer experienced the world as a place she fit into or could count on, she was certain safety could disappear without warning. At night she would wake abruptly and sit up scanning the bedroom, checking the windows, the hallway, the sounds in the house, needing to confirm that she and her husband were safe. During the day she was continually on guard, especially in parking lots and near traffic, with her attention pulled toward movement, headlights, the angle of passing cars. Already braced for catastrophe, she found that almost anything in those settings could become a warning she could not dismiss—a car edging over a line, brakes squealing outside campus, a vehicle stopped at an odd angle in the lot would all leap out at her as if the world were flagging the crash again. At times she had sudden episodes in which the crash seemed to be happening again, with a jolt of bodily certainty that made the present moment vanish. The more miserable and unmoored she felt, the more relentlessly she monitored for danger; and living that way only deepened her sense that her old self was gone for good. Feeling this endangered so often became, for Mele, its own kind of evidence that she had been permanently altered; the constant need to scan and check seemed to prove that she was no longer someone who could simply inhabit her life without fear.

Her fragmented memory also seemed to keep the sense of threat alive. Because she could not place the crash into a complete past event, isolated pieces returned as if unfinished. A glimpse of a damaged car on the side of the road, or even a photograph of two vehicles crumpled together in a news story, could pull up one bright shard of impact without context. If someone in the faculty lounge started talking about an accident on the freeway, she would feel her mind slip, unable to stay oriented in the conversation. The lack of a continuous memory made these moments feel less like recollection and more like re-entry into something still underway, which left her more watchful and more convinced that another catastrophe could break through at any moment.

That persistent alertness, in turn, seemed to worsen the way she remembered. When she tried to explain the crash in therapy, or when her husband gently asked what she had gone through, she often became visibly tense, eyes fixed, body rigid, and her account would fragment further under the pressure. The more keyed up she was, the less she could hold onto sequence; she could produce vivid snapshots but not the bridge between them. After nights spent waking repeatedly to check whether she was safe, she would come to campus already strained, and even passing references to accidents or seeing dented cars in the faculty parking lot could bring on a detached, unreal feeling, as if she were no longer fully present in her own body. In those moments, crash-related images and conversations did not register as reminders of something over; they hit her as immediate threats.

Her beliefs also made those triggers more potent. Because she had come to see herself as permanently altered, cut off, and unable to find meaning, any reminder of the collision felt like proof that this ruined version of life was now her real life. A discussion of a student’s commute or a colleague mentioning a highway pileup could make her feel suddenly separate from everyone else in the room, as if they still belonged to an ordinary world and she did not. Even seeing images of wrecked cars could provoke that drifting unreality, followed by a wave of dread and the familiar thought that happiness had ended with the crash. By this point the consequences were showing in her work and marriage: she struggled to stay present during departmental conversations when accidents came up, and at home her husband had stopped asking for details because he could see how quickly she became far away.

What finally brought Mele to seek help was not one single flare-up but the tightening sense that her life was narrowing around the crash. She was frightened by how easily she could be pulled out of the present and by how often she woke in the night to make sure she was safe. Most of all, she feared that the misery and disconnection had become permanent—that she would remain a person with no coherent story of what happened, no real place in her own life, and no way back to meaning. At the same time, she still held a cautious hope that if the crash could somehow become something she remembered rather than something she kept re-entering, she might feel like herself again.
